Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[EV-U01] Teaching order is not page order: open each concept with the problem, need or puzzle it answers, then name it, then define it. Recall the earlier idea it stands on before using it (half of the reference videos open by recalling the previous idea).
[EV-U02] Cut a topic with the strategy that fits the concept: an instrument (bond, bill, swap) - follow one of it through its life (issue, promise, risk, resale, return) and bring each term at the step that needs it; a cause or a real-vs-nominal idea - hold one small market or one product fixed and change one thing at a time; a series of rules or tools - problem, answer, its limit, the next problem; a policy goal - ask 'what does this depend on?' backwards until a lever appears, and name control of that lever; a whole and its parts - name the term where the parts disagree with the whole; a new pair of terms - teach it through a pair the learner knows; an exception - build the normal rule first, then the case that breaks it; competing definitions - test each on a small made-up country until its numbers break; a dense official definition - cut it into phrases, each phrase one step of a worked example; a national total - scale up from one person to a family to the country.
[EV-U03] History of institutions: cut at each law or committee; before each law ask the question it answers; then the law, then the institution or change it made, then the result, all on one running timeline that returns as the recap.
[EV-U04] Teach in layers and say so: first the everyday picture that is enough for anyone, then the exam layer ('UPSC ke liye thoda aur gehrai mein'); related measures (GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP; CPI, WPI, food index; headline and core) are taught as one world with one running example in which each measure is one filter, addition or subtraction on the same numbers.
[EV-U05] Successive systems, institutions and reforms (PLR to BPLR to base rate to MCLR; IFCI to the state DFIs, ICICI, IDBI and SIDBI; nationalisation to the 1991 reforms): each one enters as the fix for the previous one's named problem and leaves with the evidence that it fell short (one number: a 1.25-point cut reached loans as 0.6), which is the next one's problem. Give the lens first (a U-turn, a pendulum) before the details, and the map of categories only after the story (E58).
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.
[S1-16] Apply every economics concept in the real world first (Navin, 27 October 2026): in a chapter of the economics family, every definition, cause_effect and process item carries in its unpack a real_world_example: a place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm), actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer, worker, bank, RBI, government), real goods or money (sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI), numbers that change (before → after) and at least two steps, each mapped to a link of the concept's mechanism; then the sentence that names the term after the story, and one line on where the learner meets it in real life. The example is economically correct (the mechanism it runs is the concept's) and fits the learner's level (UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI, only from the book or a dated source). Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50, buyers 2 → 12, the price ₹65, only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation.
[S2-11] The content rule for a dense book (Navin, 5 November 2026, his "Mix" choice for the Sloman economics book: "gehra tarika sirf graph maths wale hisse par nahi ho sakta ... kisi page ka subsection ka concept bhi samjhana pade jahan galatfahmi bane, students galtiyan karte ho, kisi concept ka application ... sab thoroughly cover bhi ho jaaye"). When the course's length_rule is "content", narration time comes from what the items need, not from the page count (S2-01 stays the default): Section 1 marks every teachable item's teach_depth, "deep" with its deep_why when the video must give it the full treatment (a graph built step by step, a sum worked through, a misconception named and corrected, an application run on a real example, a box told as a story, a subtle point opened slowly), otherwise "normal"; a normal item needs about 0.25 spoken minutes, a deep item 0.75, a practice question 0.10. A topic video gets 0.8-1.4 times its items' minutes (at least 4.8-6), a video whose items need more than about 18 minutes is split and one under about 3.6 merged; the prerequisite video stays 5-8 minutes. Nothing the book teaches is dropped to fit (G-05).

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - role: what the item does in the book, so BIE teaches each line the right way: teach (the book's teaching: a statement, a
    definition, a list point, a table, a figure's content), in_text_question (a question the book puts to the student inside the
    text, "Can you explain how this conclusion could be drawn?": the film poses it and answers it), reader_talk (the book talking
    to the reader, "Let us now see how this happens", "This is a question that you may reasonably ask", "Discuss this amongst
    yourselves": the film says it in the teacher's own words), activity (something the student is asked to do: cut a section,
    collect leaves, observe under a microscope), biography (a box about a scientist's life), summary (a line of the chapter's
    summary), exercise (an end-of-chapter exercise or one of its parts), heading, caption. Lines under the SUMMARY and EXERCISES
    headings are summary and exercise.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - teach_depth and deep_why (S2-11): "deep" when the video must give this item the full treatment, with deep_why = graph (a diagram
    built step by step), numerical (a sum worked through), misconception (students get it wrong: named and corrected), application (the
    concept run on a real example), story (a box or case told as a story) or subtle (a fine point that needs slow opening); otherwise
    "normal" with deep_why "". Usually a quarter to two fifths of a page's teachable items are deep; a question item is "normal".
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;

    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
  - unpack.real_world_example (S1-16; Navin, 27 October 2026: "economic concepts ko real world mein apply karke samjhao"): in a chapter
    of the economics family, for every definition, cause_effect and process item, the concept APPLIED in an everyday Indian situation

    worker, bank, RBI, government); goods (the real goods or money: sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI); numbers (each
    {what, before, after}, written with digits: {"what": "price", "before": "₹50", "after": "₹65"}, {"what": "buyers", "before": "2",
    "after": "12"}); steps (at least two, each {step, mechanism_link}: the story step by step, and the link of the concept's mechanism

output.page_summary: Electron transport moves protons from stroma to lumen, water oxidation supplies lumen protons, and stromal NADP reduction consumes protons. The resulting high-H⁺ lumen and low-H⁺ stroma establish an electrochemical gradient. Proton return through ATP synthase couples gradient dissipation to ATP synthesis.

items.content: A closed thylakoid membrane encloses a lumen with high H⁺; the surrounding stroma has low H⁺. Light reaches P680 PS II and P700 PS I. Electron flow is shown from PS II through plastoquinone, cytochrome B6f and plastocyanin to PS I, then through Fd and FNR to NADP⁺ reduction. Water oxidation at PS II supplies lumen H⁺ and releases ½O₂. Proton movement from the stroma through the carrier pathway adds H⁺ to the lumen. Green arrows converge on lumen H⁺ and show its return through the CF₀–CF₁ ATP synthase to the stroma, accompanying ADP + Pᵢ → ATP. A wedge marks a high-to-low electrochemical potential gradient from lumen to stroma.

teacher_understanding.question: What problem does the figure solve?
teacher_understanding.answer: It connects light-driven electron transport to ATP synthesis through an intermediate proton gradient rather than showing electrons directly producing ATP.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two routes must be followed separately?
teacher_understanding.answer: Electrons follow the photosystems and electron carriers toward NADP⁺, while H⁺ accumulates in the lumen and returns through ATP synthase toward the stroma.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the figure be built for a first-time learner?
teacher_understanding.answer: Locate the membrane and its two sides first, trace electrons next, then mark proton accumulation and finally proton return with ATP formation.

items.exam_note: Practise compartment orientation and distinguish electron flow from proton flow.

terms.plain_meaning: membrane के दोनों तरफ H⁺ का फर्क बनाकर, उनके वापस बहने से ATP बनाना
terms.everyday_image: ऊपर जमा पानी नीचे आते हुए turbine चलाता है

why_chain.step: ATP formation needs a link to the energy captured by the photosystems.
Electron transport establishes a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane.
Return of protons through ATP synthase couples gradient breakdown to ATP formation.

unpack.example_or_place: Leaf → chloroplast → thylakoid membrane, separating lumen from stroma.
unpack.consequence: The gradient, not a direct electron-to-ADP transfer, connects the two processes.
unpack.visual_verb: trace electrons, accumulate protons, then channel protons outward
unpack.level_extra: NEET: lumen is proton-rich; ATP formation is on the stromal side.

items.content: Stroma (low H⁺); Stroma: the region outside the thylakoid membrane.

teacher_understanding.question: What does stroma name here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The compartment outside the thylakoid, contrasted with its enclosed lumen.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the low-H⁺ side?
teacher_understanding.answer: Outside the pink membrane, on the stromal side.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does stromal H⁺ decrease?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protons are taken up during carrier transport and are used for NADP⁺ reduction on this side.

items.exam_note: Do not reverse the stroma and lumen concentrations.

terms.everyday_image: पानी में रखी बंद थैली के बाहर का पानी

why_chain.step: To orient the gradient, identify the compartment losing protons.
Stromal proton removal makes this the low-H⁺ side.

unpack.example_or_place: Inside a chloroplast but outside its thylakoids.
unpack.consequence: Returning protons move toward this compartment.
unpack.level_extra: Low H⁺ means relatively higher pH, not absence of protons.

items.content: Thylakoid membrane: the pink boundary containing the photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the pink boundary represent?
teacher_understanding.answer: The membrane separating the lumen from the stroma and containing the machinery illustrated.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the proton gradient established?
teacher_understanding.answer: Across this membrane, with high H⁺ inside and low H⁺ outside.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the membrane limit free proton leakage?
teacher_understanding.answer: If protons could freely equilibrate across it, a gradient capable of driving ATP synthase would not be maintained.

items.exam_note: Chemiosmosis requires a membrane that maintains compartment separation.

terms.plain_meaning: thylakoid की सीमा बनाने वाली पतली परत
terms.everyday_image: पानी रोककर रखने वाली थैली की दीवार

why_chain.step: A useful gradient needs two separated compartments.
The thylakoid membrane separates lumen and stroma.

unpack.example_or_place: Membrane of a chloroplast thylakoid.
unpack.consequence: Proton return can be channelled through ATP synthase.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish the thylakoid membrane from the chloroplast envelope.

teacher_understanding.question: How does light enter the illustrated mechanism?
teacher_understanding.answer: Light is shown reaching both photosystems before electron transfer proceeds along their carrier pathways.

teacher_understanding.question: When does a photosystem electron gain energy?
teacher_understanding.answer: When absorbed light energy reaches the reaction centre and excites an electron.

items.exam_note: Both PS II and PS I receive light in this non-cyclic pathway.

terms.plain_meaning: photosystems को energy देने वाली रोशनी
terms.everyday_image: धूप से चलने वाला solar device

why_chain.step: Electron transport needs an energy input.
Both photosystems receive light in the diagram.

unpack.example_or_place: Photosystems in the thylakoid membrane.
unpack.consequence: Energy input supports electron movement and gradient formation.
unpack.visual_verb: flash light onto both reaction centres
unpack.level_extra: Do not interpret the two light arrows as proton arrows.

items.content: P680; PS II: the light-receiving photosystem associated with water oxidation and electron transfer to plastoquinone.

teacher_understanding.question: What do PS II and P680 identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: PS II is photosystem II; P680 names its reaction-centre chlorophyll, with an absorption maximum near 680 nm.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is PS II placed relative to the illustrated pathway?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the thylakoid membrane before plastoquinone, beside the water-oxidation site.

teacher_understanding.question: How are electrons lost by PS II replaced?
teacher_understanding.answer: Water oxidation supplies replacement electrons.

items.exam_note: PS II operates before PS I here; P680 is not a count of pigments.

terms.plain_meaning: PS II का light पकड़ने वाला reaction centre; 680 उसकी खास wavelength बताता है
terms.everyday_image: काम शुरू करने वाला पहला energy station

why_chain.step: The pathway needs an initial light-driven electron supply.
PS II receives light and passes electrons onward while water is oxidised nearby.

unpack.example_or_place: Thylakoid membrane, beside the lumen-side water-oxidation system.
unpack.consequence: Electron flow enters the plastoquinone pathway.
unpack.level_extra: 680 denotes wavelength in nanometres; PS numbering is not the flow order.

items.content: H₂O; ½O₂ + H⁺; Oxidation of water: water enters the PS II-associated reaction and oxygen and lumen protons are shown as products.

teacher_understanding.question: How does water oxidation help build the gradient?
teacher_understanding.answer: It releases H⁺ on the lumen side of the membrane, adding to lumen proton accumulation.

teacher_understanding.question: When is water oxidation needed in this pathway?
teacher_understanding.answer: During light-driven PS II operation, to replace electrons passed onward.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the chemical labels be read without mistaking the schematic for a balanced equation?
teacher_understanding.answer: H₂O means water, O₂ molecular oxygen, ½O₂ half a molecule-equivalent of oxygen, and H⁺ a proton. A balanced one-water oxidation half-reaction is H₂O → ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; e⁻ denotes an electron.

items.exam_note: Water splitting adds protons directly to the lumen; the figure is schematic, not a balanced equation.

terms.plain_meaning: water से electrons निकलना, जिससे oxygen और H⁺ भी मिलते हैं
terms.everyday_image: एक चीज़ टूटकर अलग-अलग हिस्से देना

why_chain.step: PS II needs replacement electrons after transferring electrons onward.
Water oxidation supplies them and releases lumen protons.
The figure shows these protons joining the lumen pool.

unpack.example_or_place: Lumen-facing side of the PS II water-oxidation machinery.
unpack.consequence: Water oxidation is another contributor to the proton gradient.
unpack.visual_verb: split water and add protons inside
unpack.level_extra: Oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from water; distinguish schematic labels from stoichiometry.

items.where_on_page: figure, between PS II and cytochrome complex
items.content: PQ; PQH₂; Plastoquinone: the membrane carrier shown taking up stromal H⁺ and connecting PS II with cytochrome B6f.

teacher_understanding.question: How does plastoquinone link electron transfer to proton transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: It accepts electrons and stromal protons, and its reduced form carries them toward the cytochrome complex, where protons are released toward the lumen.

teacher_understanding.question: When does PQ become PQH₂?
teacher_understanding.answer: When plastoquinone accepts two electrons and two protons, forming reduced plastoquinone or plastoquinol.

teacher_understanding.question: What do PQ and PQH₂ mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: PQ abbreviates plastoquinone; PQH₂ denotes its reduced, proton-carrying form. The subscript 2 refers to two hydrogen equivalents, not a unit of measurement.

items.exam_note: The H carrier couples stromal proton uptake to lumen proton release.

terms.plain_meaning: membrane में चलने वाला carrier जो electrons के साथ H⁺ भी लेता है
terms.everyday_image: एक ferry जो दो तरह का सामान साथ ले जाती है

why_chain.step: Electron movement must be coupled to moving protons between compartments.
The H carrier takes protons from the stroma while carrying electrons.
Protons are released on the lumen side when the electron is passed onward.

unpack.example_or_place: Within the thylakoid membrane between PS II and cytochrome B6f.
unpack.consequence: Electron flow increases lumen H⁺ while lowering stromal H⁺.
unpack.level_extra: PQH₂ is plastoquinol; do not confuse this carrier with plastocyanin.

items.content: Cytochrome B6f: the membrane complex between plastoquinone and plastocyanin, with a proton arrow directed into the lumen.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the labelled cytochrome complex's place in the chain?
teacher_understanding.answer: It connects the plastoquinone portion of the pathway with plastocyanin.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the nearby H⁺ arrow point?
teacher_understanding.answer: From the complex toward the lumen, showing proton delivery to the inside.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this complex connected to ATP synthesis?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its electron-transfer reactions contribute to proton translocation and thus to the gradient used by ATP synthase.

items.exam_note: Recognise cytochrome b₆f between PQ and PC.

terms.plain_meaning: electron रास्ते का membrane complex, जो H⁺ के अंदर जमा होने से जुड़ा है
terms.everyday_image: रास्ते का transfer station

why_chain.step: Electrons must move from the quinone carrier toward PS I.
The diagram places cytochrome B6f between PQ and PC and shows lumen-directed H⁺ movement.

unpack.example_or_place: Thylakoid membrane between plastoquinone and plastocyanin.
unpack.consequence: Electron transport helps store energy as a gradient.
unpack.level_extra: Conventional notation is cytochrome b₆f; this is not ATP synthase.

items.where_on_page: figure, between cytochrome B6f and PS I
items.content: PC; Plastocyanin: the electron carrier connecting cytochrome B6f to P700 PS I.

teacher_understanding.question: What does PC stand for?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plastocyanin, the carrier between the cytochrome complex and PS I.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does plastocyanin operate?
teacher_understanding.answer: On the lumen side of the thylakoid membrane, carrying electrons to PS I.

teacher_understanding.question: How is PC different from PQ in this mechanism?
teacher_understanding.answer: PC transfers electrons to PS I; PQ is the quinone carrier that also takes up and releases protons during its redox cycle.

items.exam_note: PC is plastocyanin, not plastoquinone.

terms.plain_meaning: cytochrome complex से PS I तक electron पहुँचाने वाला carrier
terms.everyday_image: अगले station तक संदेश पहुँचाने वाला runner

why_chain.step: PS I needs electrons arriving from the preceding chain.
PC bridges cytochrome B6f and PS I in the diagram.

unpack.example_or_place: Thylakoid lumen side.
unpack.consequence: Electron transport reaches PS I.
unpack.visual_verb: hand an electron to PS I
unpack.level_extra: PC is a copper-containing protein; keep this standard detail separate from the page labels.

items.content: P700; PS I: the light-receiving photosystem connected to PC on its input side and Fd on its output side.

teacher_understanding.question: What do PS I and P700 identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: PS I means photosystem I; P700 is its reaction-centre chlorophyll with an absorption maximum near 700 nm.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is PS I in this electron pathway?
teacher_understanding.answer: After plastocyanin and before ferredoxin and NADP reduction.

teacher_understanding.question: How does PS I help the final reduction step?
teacher_understanding.answer: Light re-energises electrons at PS I, enabling their onward transfer toward NADP⁺ reduction.

items.exam_note: PS I supplies the electrons used in NADP⁺ reduction.

terms.plain_meaning: PS I का reaction centre; 700 उसकी खास light wavelength बताता है
terms.everyday_image: रास्ते में energy फिर बढ़ाने वाला दूसरा station

why_chain.step: Electrons need sufficient energy for the terminal reduction pathway.
PS I receives light and sends electrons toward Fd and FNR.

unpack.example_or_place: Thylakoid membrane, between PC and the stromal acceptor pathway.
unpack.consequence: Electron flow reaches NADP reductase.
unpack.level_extra: 700 is a wavelength in nm, not the position of PS I in the chain.

items.content: Fd: the carrier between PS I and FNR on the stromal side.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Fd denote?
teacher_understanding.answer: Ferredoxin, an electron carrier associated with the acceptor side of PS I.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is Fd shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Above PS I, linking it to FNR on the stromal side.

teacher_understanding.question: How does Fd support NADPH production?
teacher_understanding.answer: Reduced ferredoxin supplies electrons to ferredoxin–NADP⁺ reductase.

items.exam_note: Fd is on the stromal acceptor side, unlike lumen-side PC.

terms.plain_meaning: ferredoxin, PS I के बाद electron आगे ले जाने वाला carrier
terms.everyday_image: अंतिम counter तक सामान पहुँचाने वाला courier

unpack.example_or_place: Stromal side of the thylakoid.
unpack.consequence: Electrons become available for NADP⁺ reduction.
unpack.level_extra: Expand Fd as ferredoxin; do not confuse it with FNR.

items.content: FNR: the enzyme connecting the Fd electron pathway with NADP⁺ reduction.

items.content: (b) As electrons move through the photosystems, protons are transported across the membrane. This happens because the primary acceptor of electron which is located towards the outer side of the membrane transfers its electron not to an electron carrier but to an H carrier. Hence, this molecule removes a proton from the stroma while transporting an electron. When this molecule passes on its electron to the electron carrier on the inner side of the membrane, the proton is released into the inner side or the lumen side of the membrane.
items.type_note: The complete paragraph explains why electron transport produces proton transfer; its location clauses are steps in that causal mechanism, not standalone structure descriptions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should moving electrons cause protons to cross the membrane?
teacher_understanding.answer: The electron is transferred to an H carrier that takes up a proton from the stroma. When it passes the electron onward on the inner side, it releases that proton into the lumen.

teacher_understanding.question: How can one carrier's journey be followed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Start at stromal proton uptake, follow electron carriage through the membrane pathway, then mark electron handover and proton release on the lumen side.

teacher_understanding.question: What do outer and inner mean here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Outer is toward the stroma; inner is toward the lumen of the thylakoid. They do not mean outside and inside the entire chloroplast.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the H carrier not merely a passive pore?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its proton uptake and release are coupled to its reduction and oxidation during electron transport, unlike a pore through which protons simply diffuse.

teacher_understanding.question: What two changes result from this single transport mechanism?
teacher_understanding.answer: A proton is removed from the stromal side and delivered to the lumen side, increasing the separation of the two proton pools.

items.exam_note: Trace stroma → H carrier → lumen. Electron transfer and proton transfer are coupled but are not identical routes.

teacher_understanding.answer: Because the enzyme lies on the stromal side, the protons required for NADP⁺ reduction are removed from the stroma.

teacher_understanding.answer: Electrons arrive from the acceptor pathway of PS I, and protons from the stroma participate in reduction by NADP reductase.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this reaction pump its consumed proton into the lumen?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. In the described reaction, proton removal from the stroma contributes by lowering stromal H⁺, rather than by delivering that proton across the membrane.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a gradient arise across the thylakoid membrane?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protons are depleted from the stroma while accumulating in the lumen, leaving different proton levels on the two sides.

teacher_understanding.question: How does lumen proton accumulation affect pH?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page states that the lumen shows a measurable decrease in pH as protons accumulate.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does more H⁺ mean lower, not higher, pH?
teacher_understanding.answer: pH varies inversely with hydrogen-ion concentration: increasing H⁺ lowers the pH value. Thus a proton-rich lumen is relatively more acidic.

teacher_understanding.question: How do lumen and stroma compare during gradient formation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The lumen accumulates protons and its pH falls; the stroma loses protons.

teacher_understanding.question: What observable consequence is specified on this page?

teacher_understanding.question: Why is forming a proton gradient not the final step in making ATP?
teacher_understanding.answer: The text identifies breakdown of the gradient as the event that leads to ATP synthesis; the stored difference must be used.

teacher_understanding.question: How is the gradient broken down?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protons move across the membrane toward the stroma; the figure shows their return through ATP synthase with ADP and Pᵢ converted to ATP.

teacher_understanding.question: How does gradient formation differ from gradient use?
teacher_understanding.answer: Formation increases the proton difference by lumen accumulation and stromal depletion; use allows proton return to the stroma and reduces that difference while ATP is made.

teacher_understanding.question: Would unrestricted proton leakage be equivalent to ATP synthase-mediated return?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Leakage would dissipate the gradient without the enzyme's energy coupling, so gradient loss alone does not guarantee ATP production.

teacher_understanding.question: What happens if a gradient is allowed to dissipate without being rebuilt?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its driving force declines, so sustained ATP synthesis requires continued gradient-generating activity.

items.exam_note: ATP synthesis uses lumen → stroma proton flow. 'Breakdown' means dissipation of a difference, not destruction of protons.
